questions.stem:
[In this question, position vectors are given relative to a fixed origin.]
At time $t$ seconds, where $t > 0$, a particle $P$ has velocity $\mathbf{v}\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$ where
$\mathbf{v} = 3t^2\mathbf{i} - 6t^{\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{j}$

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Find the speed of $P$ at time $t = 2$ seconds.
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Put $t = 2$ in $\mathbf{v}$ and use Pythagoras: $\sqrt{12^2 + (-6\sqrt{2})^2}$
A1: $\sqrt{216}, 6\sqrt{6}$ or 15 or better ($\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- (Whole question) Accept column vectors throughout apart from the answer to (b).
- M1: Need square root but -ve sign not required. Allow $\mathbf{i}$'s and/or $\mathbf{j}$'s to go missing from their $\mathbf{v}$ at $t = 2$, provided they have applied Pythagoras correctly.
- A1: cao. N.B. Correct answer with no working can score 2 marks.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
(b) Find an expression, in terms of $t$, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$, for the acceleration of $P$ at time $t$ seconds, where $t > 0$
(2)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Differentiate $\mathbf{v}$ wrt $t$ to obtain $\mathbf{a}$
A1: $6t\mathbf{i} - 3t^{-\frac{1}{2}}\mathbf{j}$ oe ($\mathrm{m\,s}^{-2}$) isw
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Both powers decreasing by 1. Allow a column vector. M0 if $\mathbf{i}$ or $\mathbf{j}$ is missing but allow recovery in (b).
- A1: cao. Do not accept a column vector.

parts.label: c
parts.text:
At time $t = 4$ seconds, the position vector of $P$ is $(\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{m}$.

(c) Find the position vector of $P$ at time $t = 1$ second.
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Integrate $\mathbf{v}$ wrt $t$ to obtain $\mathbf{r}$
A1: $\mathbf{r} = t^3\mathbf{i} - 4t^{\frac{3}{2}}\mathbf{j}\,(+\mathbf{C})$
M1: $(\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j}) = 4^3\mathbf{i} - 4 \times 4^{\frac{3}{2}}\mathbf{j} + \mathbf{C}$
A1: $(-62\mathbf{i} + 24\mathbf{j})\,(\mathrm{m})$ isw e.g. if they go on to find the distance.
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Both powers increasing by 1. M0 if $\mathbf{i}$ or $\mathbf{j}$ is missing but allow recovery.
- A1: ($\mathbf{r}$ = ) not required
- M1: Putting $\mathbf{r} = (\mathbf{i} - 4\mathbf{j})$ and $t = 4$ into their displacement vector expression which must have $\mathbf{C}$ (allow $C$) to give an equation in $\mathbf{C}$ only, seen or implied. Must have attempted to integrate $\mathbf{v}$ for this mark to be available. N.B. $\mathbf{C}$ does not need to be found and this is a method mark, so allow slips.
- A1: cao

questions.stem:
A rough plane is inclined to the horizontal at an angle $\alpha$, where $\tan\alpha = \frac{3}{4}$

A small block $B$ of mass $5\,\mathrm{kg}$ is held in equilibrium on the plane by a horizontal force of magnitude $X$ newtons, as shown in Figure 1.

The force acts in a vertical plane which contains a line of greatest slope of the inclined plane.

The block $B$ is modelled as a particle.

The magnitude of the normal reaction of the plane on $B$ is $68.6\,\mathrm{N}$.

Using the model,

parts.label: a(i)
parts.text:
(a) (i) find the magnitude of the frictional force acting on $B$,
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Resolve vertically
A1: $F$ acting UP the plane: $(\uparrow)\ F\sin\alpha + 68.6\cos\alpha = 5g$ OR $F$ acting DOWN the plane: $-F\sin\alpha + 68.6\cos\alpha = 5g$
Other possible equations from which $X$ would need to be eliminated to give an equation in $F$ only earn the M mark: $(\nwarrow)\ 68.6 = X\sin\alpha + 5g\cos\alpha$ (leads to $X = 49$ with $g = 9.8$); $F$ acting UP the plane: $(\nearrow)\ F + X\cos\alpha = 5g\sin\alpha$ OR $F$ acting DOWN the plane: $-F + X\cos\alpha = 5g\sin\alpha$; $(\rightarrow)\ F\cos\alpha + X = 68.6\sin\alpha$ OR $-F\cos\alpha + X = 68.6\sin\alpha$. The equation in $F$ only must then be correct to earn the A mark.
A1: $9.8$ (N) (49/5 is A0). N.B. If $\sin$ and $\cos$ are interchanged in all equations, this leads to an answer of $9.8$ in the wrong direction and can only score (a)(i) M1A1A0 (ii) A0
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Complete method to obtain an equation in $F$ only. For each equation used, correct no. of terms, dimensionally correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, each term that needs to be resolved must be resolved.
- A1: Correct equation in $F$ only, trig does not need to be substituted
- A1: cao (must be positive)

parts.label: a(ii)
parts.text:
(ii) state the direction of the frictional force acting on $B$.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
A1: Down the plane (Allow down or downwards or an arrow, but must appear as the answer to (a)(ii) not just on the diagram.)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- A1: cao. Note that this mark is dependent on an answer of 9.8 or -9.8 for (a)(i) from a fully correct solution unless they have used $g = 9.81$, in which case the answer will be 9.7 or – 9.7 (2sf) see SC2 below. N.B. Allow this mark, if their answer to (a)(i) is fully correct apart from a small error due to use of inaccurate trig i.e using an angle 36.9°
- SC 1: If they use $\mu R$ at any point (with an unknown $\mu$) for $F$ in part (a), can score (a)(i) max M1A1A0 (a) (ii) A1, where they must have obtained $\mu R = 9.8$ or – 9.8, from correct working.
- SC 2: If $g = 9.81$ is used consistently throughout 2(a), (leading to $X = 48.9$…and $F = 9.7$ (2sf)) can score max (a)(i) M1A1A0 (a)(ii) A1

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The horizontal force of magnitude $X$ newtons is now removed and $B$ moves down the plane.

Given that the coefficient of friction between $B$ and the plane is $0.5$

(b) find the acceleration of $B$ down the plane.
(6)
parts.mark_scheme:
N.B. If they use $R = 68.6$ in this part, the maximum they can score is M1A1M0A0M0A0. If they use $F = 9.8$ or their $F$ from (a) in this part, the maximum they can score is M1A1M0A0M0A0.
M1: Equation of motion down the plane
A1: $5g\sin\alpha - F = 5a$ (allow $(-a)$ instead of $a$)
M1: Resolve perpendicular to the plane
A1: $R = 5g\cos\alpha$
M1: $F = 0.5R$ seen
A1: $a = 1.96$ or $2.0$ or $2$ ($\mathrm{m\,s}^{-2}$) or $\frac{1}{5}g$
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Correct no.of terms, dimensionally correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, each term that needs to be resolved must be resolved.
- A1: Correct equation for their $F$.
- M1: Correct no. of terms, dimensionally correct, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, each term that needs to be resolved must be resolved. (N.B. M0 if $R = 68.6$ (N) is used in this equation)
- A1: Correct equation
- M1: Could be seen on a diagram (N.B. M0 if $R = 68.6$ (N) is used)
- A1: Cao. Must be positive.

questions.stem:
[In this question, $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$ are horizontal unit vectors.]
A particle $P$ of mass $4\,\mathrm{kg}$ is at rest at the point $A$ on a smooth horizontal plane.

At time $t = 0$, two forces, $\mathbf{F}_1 = (4\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{N}$ and $\mathbf{F}_2 = (\lambda\mathbf{i} + \mu\mathbf{j})\,\mathrm{N}$, where $\lambda$ and $\mu$ are constants, are applied to $P$

Given that $P$ moves in the direction of the vector $(3\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j})$

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $(4\mathbf{i} - \mathbf{j}) + (\lambda\mathbf{i} + \mu\mathbf{j}) = (4 + \lambda)\mathbf{i} + (-1 + \mu)\mathbf{j}$
M1: Use ratios to obtain an equation in $\lambda$ and $\mu$ only
A1: $\frac{4 + \lambda}{-1 + \mu} = \frac{3}{1}$ or $\frac{\frac{1}{4}(4+\lambda)}{\frac{1}{4}(-1+\mu)} = \frac{3}{1}$
A1*: $\lambda - 3\mu + 7 = 0$ (allow $0 = \lambda - 3\mu + 7$ but nothing else)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- (Whole question) Accept column vectors throughout
- M1: Adding the two forces, $\mathbf{i}$'s and $\mathbf{j}$'s must be collected (or must be a single column vector) seen or implied
- M1: Must be using ratios; Ignore an equation e.g. $(4+\lambda)\mathbf{i} + (-1+\mu)\mathbf{j} = 3\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}$ if they go on to use ratios. However, if they write $4+\lambda = 3$ and $-1+\mu = 1$ then $3(-1+\mu) = 3$ so $4+\lambda = 3(-1+\mu)$ with no use of a constant, it's M0. They may use the acceleration, with a factor of $\frac{1}{4}$ top and bottom, see alternative. Allow one side of the equation to be inverted
- A1: Correct equation
- A1*: Given answer correctly obtained. Must see at least one line of working, with the LH fraction 'removed'.

parts.label: b
parts.text:
At time $t = 4$ seconds, $P$ passes through the point $B$.

Given that $\lambda = 2$

(b) find the length of $AB$.
(5)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: $\lambda = 2 \Rightarrow \mu = 3$; resultant force $= (6\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})$ (N)
M1: $(6\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j}) = 4\mathbf{a}$ OR $|(6\mathbf{i} + 2\mathbf{j})| = 4a$
DM1: use of $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{u}t + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ with $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$, their $\mathbf{a}$ and $t = 4$: $\mathbf{r} = \frac{1}{2}\times\frac{(6\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})}{4}\times 4^2 = (12\mathbf{i} + 4\mathbf{j})$; or they may integrate their $\mathbf{a}$ twice with $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$ and put $t = 4$
M1: $\sqrt{12^2 + 4^2}$
Alternative 1 for the last two M marks: use of $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$, with $u = 0$, their $a$ and $t = 4$: $s = \frac{1}{2}\times\sqrt{1.5^2+0.5^2}\times 4^2$; use of Pythagoras to find magnitude of $\mathbf{a}$: $a = \sqrt{1.5^2+0.5^2}$
Alternative 2 for the last two M marks: use of $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$, with $u = 0$, their $a$ and $t = 4$: $s = \frac{1}{2}\times\left(\frac{\sqrt{6^2+2^2}}{4}\right)\times 4^2$; use of Pythagoras to find $|(6\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})|: = \sqrt{6^2+2^2}$
A1: $\sqrt{160}$, $2\sqrt{40}$, $4\sqrt{10}$ oe or $13$ or better (m)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Adding $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$ to find the resultant force, $\lambda$ and $\mu$ must be substituted. N.B. M0 if they use $\mu = 2$ coming from $-1+\mu = 1$ in part (a).
- M1: Use of $\mathbf{F} = 4\mathbf{a}$ Or $|\mathbf{F}| = 4a$, where $\mathbf{F}$ is their resultant. (including $3\mathbf{i} + \mathbf{j}$) This is an independent mark, so could be earned, for example, if they have subtracted the forces to find the 'resultant'. N.B. M0 if only using $\mathbf{F}_1$ or $\mathbf{F}_2$
- DM1: Dependent on previous M mark for Either: use of $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{u}t + \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{a}t^2$ with $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$, their $\mathbf{a}$ and $t = 4$ to produce a displacement vector Or: integrate twice, with $\mathbf{u} = \mathbf{0}$, their $\mathbf{a}$ and $t = 4$ to produce a displacement Vector Or: use of $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ with $u = 0$, their $a$ and $t = 4$ to produce a length
- M1: Use of Pythagoras, with square root, to find the magnitude of their displacement vector, $\mathbf{a}$ or $\mathbf{F}$ (M0 if only using $\mathbf{F}_1$ or $\mathbf{F}_2$) depending on which method they have used.
- A1: cao

questions.stem:
A uniform rod $AB$ has mass $M$ and length $2a$

A particle of mass $2M$ is attached to the rod at the point $C$, where $AC = 1.5a$

The rod rests with its end $A$ on rough horizontal ground.

The rod is held in equilibrium at an angle $\theta$ to the ground by a light string that is attached to the end $B$ of the rod.

The string is perpendicular to the rod, as shown in Figure 2.

parts.label: a
parts.text:
(a) Explain why the frictional force acting on the rod at $A$ acts horizontally to the right on the diagram.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: The horizontal component of $T$ acts to the left and since the only other horizontal force is friction, it must act to the right oe
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1: Any equivalent explanation

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The tension in the string is $T$

(b) show that $T = 2Mg\cos\theta$
(3)
parts.mark_scheme:

questions.stem:
A golf ball is at rest at the point $A$ on horizontal ground.

The ball is hit and initially moves at an angle $\alpha$ to the ground.

The ball first hits the ground at the point $B$, where $AB = 120\,\mathrm{m}$, as shown in Figure 3.

The motion of the ball is modelled as that of a particle, moving freely under gravity, whose initial speed is $U\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$

Using this model,

parts.label: a
parts.mark_scheme:
N.B. Could score 2/6 for any one of the 4 given equations if there is no corresponding second equation or there is an attempt but it's incorrect.
M1: Using horizontal motion
A1: (whole motion) $U\cos\alpha \times t = 120$ or (half way) $U\cos\alpha \times t = 60$
M1: Using vertical motion OR
A1: (whole motion) $U\sin\alpha \times t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2 = 0$ or (half way) $0 = U\sin\alpha - gt$
DM1: Attempt to solve problem by eliminating $t$
A1*: $U^2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha = 588$ (given answer correctly obtained with no wrong working seen; allow $588 = U^2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha$ but nothing else)
N.B. No credit given if they use the given answer from (b).
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Complete method to give equation in $U$, $\alpha$ and $t$ only, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, each term that needs to be resolved must be resolved
- A1: Correct equation
- M1: Complete method to give equation in $U$, $\alpha$ and $t$ only, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, each term that needs to be resolved must be resolved
- A1: Correct equation
- DM1: Eliminate $t$, dependent on first and second M1's

parts.label: b
parts.text:
The ball reaches a maximum height of $10\,\mathrm{m}$ above the ground.

(b) show that $U^2 = 1960$
(4)
parts.mark_scheme:
M1: Using vertical motion OR conservation of energy
A1: $0^2 = (U\sin\alpha)^2 - 2g\times 10$ or $\frac{1}{2}mU^2 - \frac{1}{2}m(U\cos\alpha)^2 = mg\times 10$
Alternative 1: if $t$ is time to top, use of $10 = \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ oe ($t = \frac{10}{7}$) to obtain an equation in $U$ and $\alpha$ only (M1); $U\sin\alpha = 14$ or $U\cos\alpha = 42$ (A1)
Alternative 2: if $t$ is time to top, use of $10 = U\sin\alpha\, t - \frac{1}{2}gt^2$ with $t = \frac{60}{U\cos\alpha}$ substituted, to obtain an equation in $U$ and $\alpha$ only (M1): $10 = U\sin\alpha\times\frac{60}{U\cos\alpha} - \frac{1}{2}g\left(\frac{60}{U\cos\alpha}\right)^2$ (A1)
DM1: attempt to solve problem by eliminating $\alpha$, e.g. $U\sin\alpha = 14 \Rightarrow U\cos\alpha = 42$, from part (a) or from using $t = \frac{10}{7}$, then square and add to give result; OR: $U^2\sin^2\alpha = 20g = 196$ and $U^2\sin\alpha\cos\alpha = 588$, divide to give $\tan\alpha = \frac{1}{3}$ then $\sin^2\alpha = \frac{1}{10}$, hence result; OR in Alternative 2: sub for $U^2$ using part (a), to give $\tan\alpha = \frac{1}{3}$ then $\sin^2\alpha = \frac{1}{10}$, hence result. N.B. Just stating that $\sin^2\alpha = \frac{1}{10}$, with no working, is DM0A0.
A1*: $U^2 = 1960$ (N.B. verification, i.e. starting with $U^2 = 1960$ and trying to work backwards, is not an acceptable method for this question.)
Official notes (completeness pass):
- M1: Complete method to give equation in $U$ and $\alpha$ only with correct no. of terms, condone sin/cos confusion and sign errors, each term that needs to be resolved must be resolved
- A1: Correct equation
- DM1: Eliminate $\alpha$ and rearrange, dependent on first M1
- A1*: Given answer correctly obtained with no wrong working seen (N.B. If they use a value for $\alpha$ (18.43.°.) they lose the final A1*)

parts.label: c
parts.text:
In a refinement to the model, the effect of air resistance is included.

The motion of the ball, from $A$ to $B$, is now modelled as that of a particle whose initial speed is $V\,\mathrm{m\,s}^{-1}$

This refined model is used to calculate a value for $V$

(c) State which is greater, $U$ or $V$, giving a reason for your answer.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme:
B1: $V$, since air resistance has to be overcome, or just 'because of air resistance' isw
Official notes (completeness pass):
- B1: Clear statement isw

parts.label: d
parts.text:
(d) State one further refinement to the model that would make the model more realistic.
(1)
parts.mark_scheme: B1: e.g. wind effects, more accurate value of $g$, spin of ball, size of ball, shape of ball, dimensions of ball, not a particle, variable acceleration, surface area of ball, humidity. Allow wind resistance and rotational resistance (ignore any mention of air resistance or drag). B0 if there is an incorrect extra e.g. mass or weight.
